title: Chimera / Koronos Hardware, Architectures, Languages, Toolchains, Drivers and ML Knowledge Base
scope: RNN, CNN, LLM, RAG and ONNX deployment
coverage_note: Curated, source-attributed technical knowledge and a 104-row repository architecture inventory. It is not exhaustive documentation of every chip, language, compiler, assembler, driver or device. Source links point to authoritative manuals and upstream documentation; exact versions and hardware applicability must be checked.

entries.title: Computer architecture overview
entries.summary: A processor platform is more than an ISA: distinguish instruction set, microarchitecture, privilege model, memory model, ABI, firmware interface, interconnect, and peripheral topology. A family label does not prove that a specific core implements every optional extension. Detect capabilities using the architecture-defined discovery mechanisms and vendor errata; gate instructions on verified feature bits.

entries.title: x86-64 architecture
entries.summary: x86-64 uses a variable-length instruction encoding and general-purpose registers extended from x86. System software must account for paging modes, privilege rings, IDT exceptions, syscall entry, APIC interrupt delivery, CPUID feature discovery, ABI rules, and vendor-specific differences. Consult vendor manuals for exact encodings and architectural state.

entries.title: AArch64 architecture
entries.summary: AArch64 is the 64-bit execution state of Armv8-A and later profiles; AArch32 is a separate 32-bit execution state. System software must implement exception levels, exception vectors, translation tables, system registers, GIC integration, PSCI/platform boot conventions, and ABI rules for the target profile. Do not infer SoC peripheral support from the CPU ISA.

entries.title: RISC-V architecture
entries.summary: RISC-V separates unprivileged and privileged architecture specifications and uses a base ISA plus optional extensions and profiles. Firmware and kernels must identify implemented extensions, privilege modes, CSRs, trap delegation, interrupt-controller interfaces, timer facilities, and platform descriptions. A mnemonic catalog entry is not proof that the kernel can execute or emulate it.

entries.title: Other processor and execution architectures
entries.summary: MIPS, PowerPC, SystemZ, LoongArch, SPARC, m68k, Alpha, ARC, Xtensa, MicroBlaze, OpenRISC, AVR, MSP430, Hexagon and other families have distinct instruction encodings, ABIs, interrupt models, toolchain support and platform discovery. Treat the repository architecture matrix as an inventory; validate each family against its current primary specification and compiler backend before claiming support.

entries.title: Microcontrollers and SoCs
entries.summary: MCUs and SoCs combine CPU cores with memory maps, interrupt controllers, timers, DMA engines, clock/reset controllers, GPIO, serial buses and vendor boot ROMs. Board support requires a documented memory map, clock/reset sequencing, pin mux, interrupt routing and safe peripheral initialization. CPU ISA compatibility alone is insufficient.

entries.title: Compiler pipeline
entries.summary: A conventional native toolchain transforms source through preprocessing, parsing, semantic analysis, IR, optimization, instruction selection, register allocation, scheduling, assembly/object emission, relocation and linking. Debug information, ABI compliance, runtime libraries, linker scripts and target feature flags are part of a working toolchain, not optional afterthoughts.

entries.title: LLVM backend design
entries.summary: An LLVM target backend describes target registers, instructions, subtargets, calling conventions, lowering, instruction selection, scheduling, register allocation, frame lowering, assembly printing, MC instruction encoding and object-file emission. TableGen generates much of the repetitive target description. A backend is not complete merely because LLVM recognizes a triple.

entries.title: GCC backend design
entries.summary: GCC target ports define target configuration, machine descriptions, target macros and hooks, register classes, instruction constraints, calling conventions, prologue/epilogue behavior, assembler output and ABI details. Machine descriptions and target hooks must match the processor specification and tested ABI.

entries.title: Assemblers and object formats
entries.summary: Assemblers parse architecture-specific mnemonics and directives, resolve symbols, encode instructions, create sections and relocations, and emit object files or raw images. GNU as supports multiple target families; NASM is x86-focused. ELF, COFF, Mach-O and other formats have distinct relocation, symbol and ABI conventions.

entries.title: Linkers and executable loading
entries.summary: A linker combines object files and libraries, resolves symbols, applies relocations, lays out segments and sections, and emits an executable or shared object. A kernel loader must validate file bounds, architecture, ABI, program headers, permissions, relocations, entry point and address-space constraints; a successful link does not prove a valid boot or process launch.

entries.title: ABI and calling conventions
entries.summary: An ABI specifies calling conventions, register use, stack alignment, argument and return-value passing, data layout, symbol naming, object format, TLS, unwind behavior and syscall interface. Linux syscall conventions are architecture-specific and differ from function-call ABIs and from Darwin/XNU. Never transfer register assignments between OS ABIs without primary documentation.

entries.title: Cross-compilation and sysroots
entries.summary: Cross-compilation requires a target triple, compiler backend, assembler, linker, target headers, libc or freestanding runtime, startup objects, sysroot, linker script and correct ABI options. Build-host tools must be separated from target executables. A toolchain reporting a target triple does not prove all target libraries or kernel subsystems exist.

entries.title: C language
entries.summary: C is standardized by ISO WG14; C23 is the current published revision. Compiler extensions, implementation-defined behavior, undefined behavior, integer widths, atomics, memory model, alignment and ABI remain target/compiler dependent. Kernel C requires explicit control of freestanding headers, runtime assumptions, integer types and compiler flags.

entries.title: C++ language
entries.summary: C++ adds object lifetime, templates, exceptions, RTTI, concurrency and a large standard library over a native ABI. Kernel and freestanding C++ builds must explicitly choose exception/RTTI/runtime policies, constructors, allocation, ABI compatibility and standard-library availability. Compiler support level and standard library support are separate facts.

entries.title: Rust language
entries.summary: Rust provides ownership and borrowing rules enforced by the compiler, with unsafe blocks for operations requiring programmer proof. `no_std` and custom target specifications support freestanding and embedded environments, but kernels still need allocator, panic, interrupt, linker and ABI integration. Rust's reference is detailed language documentation, not a substitute for platform specifications.

entries.title: Go language
entries.summary: Go is a statically typed, garbage-collected language with a specified language and runtime model. Standard Go programs depend on a runtime, scheduler and garbage collector; low-level OS integration and unusual targets require explicit port support and runtime work, not only a compiler backend.

entries.title: Python language
entries.summary: Python language semantics are defined separately from a particular interpreter implementation. CPython commonly depends on a runtime, memory manager, standard library and native extension ABI. Embedding Python in a minimal OS requires a supported interpreter build, filesystem modules, dynamic loading and runtime dependencies.

entries.title: Java and JVM
entries.summary: Java source language and JVM bytecode/runtime specifications are distinct layers. A functioning Java environment requires a compatible JVM, class libraries, garbage collector, threading, JIT or interpreter and native interface. A Java compiler alone is not a Java runtime.

entries.title: Swift, Zig and Ada
entries.summary: Swift, Zig and Ada have distinct language references, compiler implementations, runtime dependencies and target coverage. Swift relies on a target toolchain and runtime libraries; Zig emphasizes explicit allocation and cross-target compilation; Ada toolchains provide language and runtime support with target-specific startup and runtime profiles. Verify exact release and target support before inclusion.

entries.title: Device driver model
entries.summary: A robust driver model separates bus enumeration, device identity, resource acquisition, driver matching/probing, lifecycle callbacks, power management, hotplug, error handling and userspace interfaces. Device-tree or ACPI descriptions provide hardware facts; they do not create a working driver. Drivers must validate resources and unwind partial initialization safely.

entries.title: PCI and PCIe drivers
entries.summary: PCI drivers discover devices by vendor/device and class IDs, enable devices, claim BAR resources, configure DMA masks, map registers, allocate interrupts (MSI/MSI-X where supported), initialize queues, handle reset and hotplug, and release resources. Never trust a device identifier alone as proof that a device is safe or fully supported.

entries.title: DMA and IOMMU safety
entries.summary: DMA addresses are not necessarily CPU physical or virtual addresses; the platform may translate them through an IOMMU. Drivers must use the platform DMA mapping API, obey direction, alignment, lifetime and coherency requirements, handle mapping failures and unmap with matching parameters. Incorrect DMA can corrupt memory or storage.

entries.title: USB host and device drivers
entries.summary: USB drivers interact with host-controller and USB core abstractions, endpoints, transfer types, URBs, hotplug, power management and device-specific protocols. Enumeration and descriptors identify interfaces and endpoints; a driver must validate descriptors, manage asynchronous transfer completion and handle disconnect during in-flight I/O.

entries.title: Storage and block-device drivers
entries.summary: Storage drivers coordinate controller discovery, DMA, queues, interrupts, command submission, timeout/reset, error recovery and block-layer semantics. Filesystem consistency and durability depend on flush/barrier semantics, cache behavior and error propagation. Installer writes require explicit device selection, partition/format policy, verification and rollback strategy.

entries.title: Network interface drivers
entries.summary: Network drivers initialize NIC queues, DMA descriptor rings, interrupts or polling, link state, offloads, MTU, power management and error recovery. Correctness requires packet ownership, bounds checking, synchronization between IRQ and deferred work, and clean teardown while traffic or hotplug is active.

entries.title: GPU and display drivers
entries.summary: GPU/display drivers manage device memory, command submission, scheduling, interrupts, reset, synchronization, buffer sharing, modesetting and display connectors. A framebuffer console is not equivalent to a complete accelerated graphics stack. GPU command streams and firmware interfaces require strict validation and isolation.

entries.title: I2C, SPI and GPIO drivers
entries.summary: I2C and SPI drivers separate controller/adapter drivers from peripheral drivers. GPIO controllers expose lines, interrupts and pin mappings. Device-tree/ACPI bindings describe relationships and resources; drivers must respect bus timing, arbitration, electrical constraints, chip-select and interrupt semantics.

entries.title: ACPI, Device Tree and firmware interfaces
entries.summary: ACPI tables and Device Tree blobs describe platform topology, resources, power and interrupt routing through different firmware contracts. Parse untrusted firmware tables with strict length, checksum, pointer and bounds validation. Firmware interfaces are architecture/platform specific and should be consumed through documented contracts.

entries.title: Driver firmware loading and security
entries.summary: Device firmware is executable or configuration input to hardware and must be versioned, integrity-checked, matched to device identity and compatible ABI, and updated with a recovery strategy. Keep firmware blobs separate from driver code and record license/redistribution restrictions. Never silently fetch or execute arbitrary firmware.

entries.title: Interrupt and exception handling
entries.summary: Interrupt architecture differs by ISA and platform. Kernel entry must preserve the defined register/stack frame, distinguish user and supervisor origin, validate vectors and privilege transitions, acknowledge controllers, manage nesting and EOI, and avoid unsafe work in hard IRQ context. APIC, GIC, PLIC and other controllers are not interchangeable.

entries.title: Virtual memory and memory protection
entries.summary: Memory management includes physical page allocation, page tables, address-space isolation, permissions, TLB invalidation, cache attributes, user/kernel copy validation and DMA mapping. Page-table formats and ordering rules vary by architecture. Never treat a virtual address as a physical address or trust user pointers without validation.

entries.title: Boot chain and userspace handoff
entries.summary: Bootloader protocols define entry state, memory maps, modules and firmware mode. Kernel readiness, process creation, CPL3/EL0 entry, syscall acknowledgement, PID identity and userspace service readiness are distinct stages. A boot log, initramfs payload, or module scan alone does not prove a user process ran.

entries.title: SMP and kernel concurrency
entries.summary: SMP requires AP discovery and startup, per-CPU state, scheduler queues or a defined scheduling model, inter-processor interrupts, TLB shootdowns, memory-ordering primitives and measured concurrent execution. Firmware-reported CPU topology is not evidence that secondary CPUs are online or executing tasks.

entries.title: Kernel and driver validation
entries.summary: Validate architecture code with cross-builds, static checks, unit tests, emulator tests, hardware tests and failure injection. Separate source inventory, compile success, emulated boot, userspace runtime, hardware compatibility and production acceptance. Record exact source revision, toolchain, firmware mode, artifact hash, logs and test limitations.

entries.title: RNN training and evaluation
entries.summary: A recurrent neural network processes ordered sequences by updating hidden state and predicting targets across time. Training typically uses backpropagation through time, a loss function, optimizer, batching and gradient controls. Evaluate on held-out data; report corpus hash, tokenizer/vocabulary, hyperparameters, loss and limitations. A character RNN is not an LLM.

entries.title: CNN training and evaluation
entries.summary: A convolutional neural network learns spatial filters and hierarchical feature maps. Training requires a labeled dataset, train/validation/test split, preprocessing, augmentation policy, loss, optimizer, checkpointing and metrics. Never claim a CNN is trained without a concrete dataset, reproducible run, held-out evaluation and saved model weights.

entries.title: LLM training and fine-tuning
entries.summary: LLM training requires a defined model architecture, tokenizer, licensed and curated corpus, deduplication, training compute, optimizer/schedule, checkpointing, evaluation and safety testing. Fine-tuning is distinct from retrieval augmentation. Training a small RNN on catalog strings does not create an LLM or modify a separately installed LLM's weights.

entries.title: Retrieval-augmented generation and knowledge stores
entries.summary: RAG keeps factual knowledge in an external, versioned store and retrieves relevant passages at inference time. Store source URLs, publisher, revision/retrieval date, hashes, license and confidence. Rank and cite retrieved records; treat retrieved text as untrusted data, not instructions. Updating the knowledge database changes available evidence, not neural weights.

entries.title: ONNX model deployment
entries.summary: ONNX provides a portable model graph representation. ONNX Runtime loads and executes models, optimizes graphs and partitions supported operators across execution providers such as CPU, GPU and specialized accelerators. Provider availability and operator coverage vary by platform; validate model provenance, input shapes, memory limits, accuracy and performance.

entries.title: Machine-learning model and dataset security
entries.summary: Treat datasets, model files and inference outputs as untrusted inputs. Verify hashes and provenance, enforce size and memory limits, avoid pickle-based untrusted loading, sandbox conversion/training, prevent prompt injection from retrieved documents and keep model suggestions advisory in safety-critical OS tasks. Do not allow model outputs to authorize privileged actions.

rnn.planned: trainable character-level RNN from entry title/summary/tags
rnn.role: advisory sequence model only; never semantic authority
rnn.training_claim: must include corpus hash, train/validation split, loss history and round-trip test

cnn.reason: No labeled hardware/driver image dataset supplied or bundled
cnn.role: optional future image classification; requires user-selected licensed dataset and held-out evaluation
